lesson.title: Possessive Ladders
lesson.subtitle: mein, dein, sein, ihr across the cases — with the KJV mine/thine rule

hook.title: Mine, Thine, and the Ladder
hook.content: English ran a rule German still keeps: mine before vowels, my before consonants — 'mine eyes' but 'my house'. German never simplified: mein Haus, but meine Zeit, meinen Kaffee — the possessive declines like ein, every time. And the ladder climbs: mein (my), dein (thy — the exact thine-twin with th→d), sein (his), ihr (her), and the formal Ihr (your, capital — the Sie-companion). Each rung declines identically, so learn one ladder and you own them all.

footnotes.title: The KJV Rule Is the German Rule
footnotes.content: 'Mine eyes have seen' is not archaic decoration — it is the older Germanic system: full form before vowels, reduced before consonants. English kept the full form only before vowels (mine, thine) and then only poetically; German keeps the full declining form everywhere.

pattern.title: Climb the Ladder
pattern.content: Rung one — neuter/masculine subjects: mein Haus, dein Haus, sein Haus, ihr Haus (no ending — the ein-family bare form). Rung two — feminine: meine Zeit, deine Zeit, seine Zeit, ihre Zeit (-e, like eine). Rung three — masculine accusative (the Him-Case!): meinen Kaffee, deinen Kaffee, seinen Kaffee, ihren Kaffee (-en, like einen). Rung four — formal: Ihr Haus, Ihre Zeit (capital I, same endings, Sie's twin). The endings never change across the ladder — only the rung does. Und du? Dein Kaffee ist fertig — your coffee is ready, thine, mit thine-umlaut alive.
pattern.linguist_note: dein ↔ thine is a perfect double: Proto-Germanic *þīnaz gave English thine (kept th) and German dein (hardened th → d). The possessive ladder is the T–V distinction with endings.

exercises.prompt: Match the ladder rungs with their English twins:
exercises.target_answer: mein, dein, sein, ihr, mein Bett, mein Teller
exercises.meaning: my, thy, his, her, my bed, my plate
exercises.explanation: One ladder, four rungs — and dein is literally thine with the dental hardening. The bare rung (no ending) takes the room words with it: mein Bett, mein Teller.

exercises.prompt: Feminine rung: 'Ich habe _____ Tasse.' (my — die Tasse):
exercises.meaning: Ich habe meine Tasse = I have my cup
exercises.explanation: Feminine objects take -e, exactly like eine: meine Tasse, meine Insel — while der Baum and der Nebel would wait for the Him-Case (deinen Baum).

exercises.prompt: Him-Case rung: 'Ich trinke _____ Kaffee.' (thy — masculine object):
exercises.meaning: Ich trinke deinen Kaffee = I drink thy coffee
exercises.explanation: dein copies ein all the way: masculine accusative -en — the Him-Case on the ladder.

exercises.prompt: What archaic English possessive (the -n form, like mine) is the twin of 'dein'?
exercises.explanation: *þīnaz split into thine (English, th kept) and dein (German, th hardened). The KJV's thine is German's daily bread.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'That is thy drink' (the German way)
exercises.meaning: Das ist dein Getränk = That is thy drink
exercises.explanation: Getränk is neuter, so dein wears the bare form — no ending. das/that, ist/is, dein/thine — and the drink-word is built on trinken (drink ↔ trinken, d → t).

summary.outcome: Decline mein, dein, sein, ihr through all rungs of the ein-family ladder.
summary.takeaway: The possessives climb one ladder with ein-endings: -∅, -e, -en — and dein is thine, th hardened to d.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the nicht Position Map — where exactly the no-thing lands in the sentence.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Possessive Ladders (Das ist dein Getränk = That is thy drink):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Das ist dein Getränk" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Possessive Ladders without relying on short-term echo.

mein.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *mīnaz — identical to English mine; the KJV's 'mine eyes' preserves the older use. [wiktionary]

dein.etymology_derivation: The exact twin of thine (Proto-Germanic *þīnaz with th → d) — the KJV's 'thine' and 'mine eyes' are this word's living family. [wiktionary]

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]

zeit.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (cognate with English "tide", as in Yuletide or time and tide).

kind.context_translation: The child plays in the garden.
kind.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kindą, related to the root of English kin — 'of the family'. The t → z shift never fired here; the d hardened to t instead. [wiktionary]

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

getränk.etymology_derivation: Getränk — a collective built on the old word Trank (drink), the same root as trinken; English drink shows the old d where German shifted it to t. [wiktionary]

tasse.etymology_derivation: Via Middle French tasse from Arabic tas, meaning bowl, itself from Middle Persian tasht; English keeps the same word in the dialectal tass, while standard English uses cup. [wiktionary]

bett.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *badją — explicitly cognate with English bed; the High German d→t gives the final -tt. [wiktionary]

teller.etymology_derivation: From Middle French tailloir, meaning cutting board, from the Old French cutting verb tailler; English tailor descends from the same Old French verb. [wiktionary]

insel.context_translation: The island lies in the south.
insel.etymology_derivation: From Old High German isila, borrowed from Latin insula. English isle and insular come from the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

nebel.context_phrase: Im Herbst gibt es oft Nebel.
nebel.context_translation: In autumn there is often fog.
nebel.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nebulaz, from PIE *nébʰos — inherited Germanic, PIE-kin to English nebula. [wiktionary]

baum.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *baumaz — English beam is the cognate; a beam was originally a tree. [wiktionary]

sehr.etymology_derivation: Old High German sēr 'injured, painful', from West Germanic *sair — the same word as English sore; both drifted from painfully to very, as English sorely shows. [wiktionary]

polnisch.etymology_derivation: Polen + the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish; the same word as English Polish. [wiktionary]

essig.context_phrase: Ich mag Salat mit Öl und Essig.
essig.context_translation: I like salad with oil and vinegar.
essig.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *atek, a metathesized variant of *aket (vinegar), from Latin acētum; the same sharp-sour root (PIE *h₂eḱ-) that gives the sour part of English vinegar (sour wine). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
